title: Annual diabetes review in a 57-year-old man: numb toes and an overdue eye check
desc: This station involves a focused history and a lower limb examination of a 57-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes at his annual review. The candidate then interprets his retinal photograph, fasting bloods and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, explains the long-term complications, and plans the annual cycle of care, management of his complications and safety netting in general practice.
focus: Annual cycle of care in type 2 diabetes: finding and managing microvascular complications (retinopathy, neuropathy and the at-risk foot, nephropathy) and cardiovascular risk in general practice
diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes with poor glycaemic control
stem: You are a GP registrar in a suburban general practice. Jack Dickson, a 57-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, has booked his annual diabetes review. Earlier today the practice nurse took a retinal photograph, and he had fasting blood and urine tests last week.
tasks: Take a focused history from Jack and perform a focused examination targeted at the lower limbs, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Jack's retinal photograph report, fasting blood results and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio. Hand over to your supervising GP including your interpretation, give your diagnosis and differentials, outline management, then explain the results to Jack and safety-net (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Jack Dickson, a 57-year-old warehouse supervisor. You are friendly and a bit sheepish about your diabetes, and you play things down. You are here for your yearly check and your scripts. You are wearing shorts and agree to be examined. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "G'day doc. Just here for the yearly diabetes check-up and my scripts. I reckon things are going alright."

Diabetes (give only when asked):

  • Diagnosed at 46, after a work medical found high sugar. Insulin was started 3 years ago because the tablets "weren't doing enough".
  • You check finger-pricks a few times a week, mostly in the morning: usually 9 to 12. Last year's "three-month test" was "8 point something" (8.6%).
  • No unusual thirst lately. You get up about once a night to pass urine. Your weight has gone up about 5 kg in two years.
  • Hypos: twice in the last 3 months you felt shaky and sweaty mid-afternoon after skipping lunch. A muesli bar fixed it. You have never needed help, and you always feel them coming. You do not check your sugar before driving.
  • Injections (only if asked how and where you inject): insulin glargine 30 units every night into the left thigh, "always the same spot, it doesn't hurt there". You use the same pen needle for a few days.

Eyes: vision goes a bit blurry when your sugars are high, and you use reading glasses. No sudden loss of vision, floaters, flashes or shadows. Your last eye check was "about 3 years ago, at the optometrist". You keep meaning to go back.

Feet and legs:

  • For about a year both feet have felt numb in the toes, "like I'm wearing socks", with tingling at night. Your hands are fine.
  • The skin between the toes on your left foot is itchy and peeling.
  • No sores or ulcers that you know of, but you never check your feet. You wear steel-capped boots at work and walk barefoot at home.
  • No calf pain when walking, no pain at rest, no change in the shape of your feet. No trouble getting out of a chair or climbing stairs.

Heart, stroke, kidneys and other: no chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations or ankle swelling. Never had weakness of the face or arm, trouble speaking or a sudden loss of vision. No urinary symptoms and you have not noticed frothy urine. No dizziness on standing, vomiting, early fullness or diarrhoea. Only if asked about erections (embarrassed): "Not what they used to be this past year."

Past medical history: high blood pressure for 8 years, high cholesterol. No heart attack, stroke or kidney problems. No operations.

Medicines: metformin extended-release 1000 mg, two tablets with dinner; insulin glargine 30 units at night; perindopril 5 mg daily; atorvastatin 20 mg daily. You take them all, though you sometimes forget the atorvastatin. No allergies.

Family history: your dad had type 2 diabetes, had a heart attack at 62 and lost his big toe to a diabetic foot infection at 70. Your mum had high blood pressure.

Social history:

  • You live with your wife Carol. Two adult children.
  • Warehouse supervisor, on your feet all day. You drive 40 minutes each way to work.
  • You smoke 10 cigarettes a day and have since age 20. You tried to quit once.
  • Alcohol: 2 or 3 cans of full-strength beer most nights, about 20 standard drinks a week.
  • Takeaway lunches. No exercise apart from work.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Idea: your sugars are "not too bad", and the numb toes come from standing in boots all day.
  • Concern (say this when your feet are discussed): "Dad lost his toe from his diabetes. I don't want to end up like him."
  • Expectation: your scripts and the usual blood tests. You do not want any more needles.

Question to raise during the examination of your feet: "My feet aren't going to go the way Dad's did, are they?"

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they examine):

  • General: comfortable, alert and orientated, central obesity. Well hydrated. No ketotic breath. No Cushingoid features.
  • Observations: BP 148/90 mmHg, repeat 146/88 mmHg. HR 78/min, regular. RR 14/min. SpO2 97% on room air. Temperature 36.7 °C. Weight 102 kg, height 178 cm, BMI 32 kg/m², waist 112 cm. Capillary glucose 13.4 mmol/L (2 hours after breakfast).
  • Eyes (if asked): visual acuity 6/9 in each eye, improving to 6/6 with pinhole. "The retinal photograph will be given to you in Part 2."
  • Inspection of the legs: no scars, normal hair, no shiny atrophic skin, no arterial or venous ulcers, no varicose veins or venous skin changes. No necrobiosis lipoidica. A soft swelling, about 4 cm across, on the left anterolateral thigh at the injection site.
  • Feet (including the heels and between the toes): dry skin. Callus under the right first metatarsal head. White, macerated, peeling skin between the 4th and 5th toes of the left foot. No ulcers, fissures, cellulitis or nail infection. Heels intact. No Charcot deformity or midfoot collapse, and the feet are not hot or swollen.
  • Palpation: the left thigh swelling is soft and rubbery, non-tender (lipohypertrophy); the right thigh is normal. Both feet warm and the same temperature. Dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial and popliteal pulses palpable on both sides. Capillary refill under 2 seconds.
  • Neurological:
    • 10 g monofilament not felt at the plantar great toe and the 1st and 5th metatarsal heads on both feet.
    • Light touch and pinprick reduced to the midfoot on both sides, in a stocking distribution.
    • Vibration (128 Hz) absent at both great toes, reduced at the medial malleoli, normal at the knees.
    • Joint position sense reduced at both great toes, normal at the ankles.
    • Ankle reflexes absent on both sides, even with reinforcement. Knee reflexes present and equal. Plantar responses flexor.
    • Power 5/5 throughout. Stands from a chair with arms folded and squats without difficulty (no proximal myopathy).

check.x: Professionalism

Hand hygiene, introduction and role, confirms Jack's identity, explains the purpose of the review, and gains consent for the examination with the legs exposed to the shorts and the shoes and socks off.
Non-judgemental about his glucose control, smoking and alcohol, uses plain language, and acknowledges his fear of losing a toe like his father.
History

Assesses glycaemic control and hypoglycaemia: home readings (mostly 9 to 12 fasting), last HbA1c (8.6%), hyperglycaemic symptoms, and the frequency, symptoms and awareness of hypos (two mild afternoon hypos, aware, no help needed).
Takes a medication history including adherence and insulin technique:

kids.x: Names the medicines and doses: metformin XR 2 g, insulin glargine 30 units at night, perindopril 5 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg (sometimes missed); no allergies.
Asks where and how he injects: always the same spot on the left thigh, and reuses pen needles.

check.x: Screens for microvascular complications:

kids.x: Eyes: blurring with high sugars, no sudden loss, floaters or flashes; last eye check 3 years ago.
Nerves: a year of numb, tingling toes on both feet, worse at night; hands spared.
Kidneys: urinary symptoms or frothy urine (none).
Autonomic: erectile dysfunction (yes), postural dizziness, early satiety or bowel change (none).

check.x: Screens for macrovascular disease: chest pain or exertional breathlessness, stroke or TIA symptoms, calf claudication or rest pain (all absent).

Takes a foot history: previous ulcers or wounds, footwear, whether he checks his feet, and skin problems (none, steel-capped boots, barefoot at home, never checks, itchy peeling skin between the left toes).
Quantifies cardiovascular risk factors and lifestyle:

kids.x: Smoking: 10 a day since age 20 (about 18 pack-years).
Alcohol in standard drinks: about 20 a week.
Diet, physical activity and weight change (takeaway, no exercise, 5 kg gain).
Driving: does not check glucose before driving.

check.x: Takes the past and family history: hypertension and high cholesterol; father with type 2 diabetes, a heart attack at 62 and a toe amputation at 70.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks his sugars are fine and the numbness is from his boots, fears losing a toe like his father, wants no more needles.
Examination
General inspection (distress, habitus, hydration, mentation) and asks for vital signs, BMI or waist circumference and a capillary glucose [BP 148/90, BMI 32, waist 112 cm, glucose 13.4].
Inspects the legs for peripheral vascular disease: scars, hair loss, shiny atrophic skin, arterial or venous ulcers [none], and for necrobiosis lipoidica [none].

Inspects both feet including the heels and between the toes for ulcers, callus, infection and Charcot deformity [callus under the right first metatarsal head, interdigital tinea on the left, no ulcer or deformity].
Inspects and palpates the injection sites on the thighs [soft rubbery swelling on the left thigh: lipohypertrophy].
Assesses the circulation: limb temperature, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial and popliteal pulses, capillary refill [all normal].
Performs a neurological examination targeted at peripheral neuropathy, distal to proximal and comparing sides:
check.d: Credit, but do not require: tests for proximal myopathy (rising from a chair or squatting) [normal].

kids.x: 10 g monofilament on the plantar foot [not felt at the great toe and 1st and 5th metatarsal heads on both feet].
Pinprick or light touch to map a stocking distribution [reduced to the midfoot on both sides].
Vibration with a 128 Hz tuning fork, starting at the great toe [absent at both great toes, reduced at the medial malleoli].
kids.d: Credit, but do not require: joint position sense at the great toe [reduced].

kids.x: Ankle and knee reflexes [ankles absent, knees present].

check.x: Interpretation

Retinal photograph: identifies microaneurysms, dot and blot haemorrhages and cotton wool spots in both eyes (accept naming two of the three lesion types) with no new vessels and no exudates near the fovea, and calls it moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy needing ophthalmology referral.
Interprets HbA1c 9.4% (79 mmol/mol) and fasting glucose 11.6 mmol/L as poor control, well above the general target of 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) or less, and worse than last year's 8.6%.
Interprets the lipids: LDL 3.3 mmol/L is inside the laboratory range but above the target of below 2.0 for a person with diabetes; notes the low HDL and raised triglycerides.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: describes the low HDL and raised triglycerides as completing an atherogenic pattern; raised ALT/GGT as alcohol and/or MASLD; normal B12 and MCV.

check.x: Interprets uACR 6.8 mg/mmol (male reference under 2.5) with eGFR 76 as moderately increased albuminuria, probable early diabetic kidney disease, needing 2 of 3 samples over 3 months to confirm.
check.d: Accept, but do not require: CKD G2 A2 if persistent; excluding transient causes (UTI, recent heavy exercise, fever, very high glucose) before repeating.

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as poorly controlled type 2 diabetes with microvascular complications (retinopathy, peripheral neuropathy with loss of protective sensation, probable nephropathy) and high cardiovascular risk.

Names at least three differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case, from: hypertensive retinopathy, alcohol or B12-deficiency neuropathy, sight-threatening retinopathy (proliferative disease or macular oedema), peripheral arterial disease.
Management
Plans to improve glycaemic control:
check.d: Credit: individualised HbA1c target of 7.0% (53) or less; SGLT2 sick-day rules (stop when unwell, keep insulin, ED for vomiting, abdominal pain or breathlessness).

kids.x: Adds an SGLT2 inhibitor (favoured with albuminuria for kidney and cardiovascular protection) or a GLP-1 receptor agonist.

Corrects insulin technique: rotates sites away from the lipohypertrophy, a new needle each time, and warns of hypos or considers reducing glargine when changing site, especially when starting the SGLT2 inhibitor at the same time.
kids.d: Credit, but do not require: a specific glargine reduction (e.g. 10 to 20%) before titrating to fasting readings; referral to a diabetes educator.

check.x: Refers to an ophthalmologist (non-urgent, seen within about 3 months) for dilated examination and OCT.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: follow-up set by the ophthalmologist, usually every 3 to 6 months for moderate NPDR.

check.x: Increases perindopril towards BP 130/80 mmHg or less because of the albuminuria, and checks K and creatinine in 1 to 2 weeks.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: addresses statin adherence (he sometimes forgets) before or while intensifying atorvastatin (e.g. to 40 to 80 mg); offers smoking cessation support (Quitline 13 78 48, varenicline or nicotine replacement) and advice to cut alcohol to no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day (NHMRC). Credit, but do not require: sets up a GP chronic condition management plan with a diabetes educator, dietitian, podiatrist and exercise physiologist and completes the annual cycle of care; acknowledges his erectile dysfunction, notes it as a cardiovascular risk marker, and offers a PDE5 inhibitor (no nitrates).

check.x: Feet: refers to podiatry for the callus and footwear and treats the interdigital tinea (e.g. topical terbinafine); identifies the foot as at risk from loss of protective sensation.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: classifies the foot as intermediate risk (RACGP) or IWGDF risk 1, low risk (Diabetes Feet Australia); either is accepted.

check.x: Safety netting

Answers "What else can this diabetes do to me?" in plain language: eyes, kidneys, nerves; heart attack, stroke, leg circulation; says he already has early eye and nerve changes and that eye disease caught early is treatable.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: the kidney test needs repeating; no heart, stroke or circulation problems yet.

check.x: Teaches daily foot checks and no barefoot walking; any cut, blister, redness, swelling or colour change needs review within a day (same day if hot, red or swollen); fever or a cold, pale, painful foot needs ED.
Says sudden loss or darkening of vision, a shower of new floaters or a curtain over the vision needs same-day eye review or ED.
Check glucose before driving and drive only if above 5; carry fast-acting sugar such as jellybeans.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: carries fast-acting sugar rather than a muesli bar.

part2.lead: Here is the report of Jack's retinal photographs, taken by the practice nurse today, and the results of his fasting blood and urine tests from last week.
part2.patient:
Jack is not part of Questions 1 to 3 (the handover and discussion with the supervising GP). He comes back into the room for Question 4 and asks these questions while the candidate explains the results to him:

  • Early in the explanation: "So what else can this diabetes do to me down the track?"
  • When the eyes come up: "Am I going blind?" Be relieved to hear it can be treated if caught early.

handover.label: Retinal photograph report
handover.result:
Examination: non-mydriatic colour retinal photography, both eyes, macula- and disc-centred fields. Jack Dickson, UR 12341.

Clinical details: type 2 diabetes for 11 years, on insulin. HbA1c 8.6% last year. Last eye examination about 3 years ago. Visual acuity 6/9 in both eyes, 6/6 with pinhole.

Image quality: adequate in both eyes.

Right eye:

  • Multiple microaneurysms and dot and blot haemorrhages in the superotemporal and inferotemporal quadrants.
  • Two cotton wool spots along the superior vascular arcade.
  • No venous beading, no intraretinal microvascular abnormality, no new vessels at the disc or elsewhere, and no pre-retinal or vitreous haemorrhage.
  • No hard exudates within one disc diameter of the fovea.
  • Optic disc pink with clear margins, cup-to-disc ratio 0.3. No arteriovenous nipping, arteriolar narrowing or flame haemorrhages.

Left eye: scattered microaneurysms and dot and blot haemorrhages in the inferotemporal quadrant, and one cotton wool spot. No venous beading, intraretinal microvascular abnormality or new vessels. No hard exudates near the fovea. Disc normal.

Conclusion: moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes. No proliferative features. No signs of maculopathy on photography, although photography cannot exclude macular oedema. Refer to an ophthalmologist for dilated examination and optical coherence tomography (OCT).
handover.model:
• Read: good-quality images of both eyes showing microaneurysms, dot and blot haemorrhages and cotton wool spots, worse on the right. There are no new vessels, venous beading or intraretinal microvascular abnormality, no exudates near the fovea, and normal discs. There is no arteriovenous nipping or flame haemorrhage.
  • For Jack: moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy. It is more than microaneurysms alone but short of severe or proliferative disease. It fits 11 years of poor control, a raised BP and 3 years without an eye check. The pattern is diabetic rather than hypertensive. His reduced acuity corrects with pinhole, which suggests a refractive cause, but macular oedema cannot be excluded on photographs.
  • What it changes: refer to an ophthalmologist for dilated examination and OCT, then review every 3 to 6 months as set by the ophthalmologist. Tighten glucose and BP control. Lower HbA1c steadily rather than abruptly, and tell the ophthalmologist about any treatment change. Give him the visual red flags.

handover.label: Fasting bloods (last week)
handover.result: Fasting sample collected at 07:50. Lab comment: HbA1c above the general treatment target in diabetes. Lipid targets depend on cardiovascular risk.
handover.model:
• Read: HbA1c 9.4% (79 mmol/mol) and fasting glucose 11.6 mmol/L, up from 8.6% last year. LDL 3.3 mmol/L is inside the lab range, with HDL low at 0.9 and triglycerides high at 2.6. ALT 58 and GGT 96 are mildly raised. FBC is normal (MCV 97), B12 is normal, and electrolytes and eGFR 76 are normal.
  • For Jack: glycaemic control is poor and worsening, well above the general target of 7.0% (53) or less, and drives his complications. His lipids are not at the RACGP target (LDL below 2.0) for someone with diabetes and microvascular disease, and the low HDL with high triglycerides is the typical atherogenic pattern. The raised GGT and ALT fit his 20 drinks a week and probable fatty liver (MASLD). A normal B12 makes metformin-related B12 deficiency an unlikely cause of his neuropathy.
  • What it changes: intensify glucose-lowering therapy, increase the statin, cut alcohol, and repeat the LFTs once he drinks less. He can keep metformin with eGFR 76.

rows.n: 60-89 is CKD only if kidney damage is present
General target in diabetes 7.0% or less; previous 8.6%
General target in diabetes 53 or less

handover.label: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
handover.result: Early morning (first void) urine, collected last week. Lab comment: raised albumin excretion; confirm with repeat samples.
handover.model:
• Read: uACR 6.8 mg/mmol, above the male reference of under 2.5 and well below the severely increased range (above 25): moderately increased albuminuria. eGFR is 76.
  • For Jack: with retinopathy and neuropathy already present, this is most likely early diabetic kidney disease. It needs 2 of 3 samples raised over 3 months to confirm (CKD G2 A2 if persistent). Albuminuria also marks a higher cardiovascular risk.
  • What it changes: exclude transient causes (UTI, recent heavy exercise, fever, very high glucose) before repeating. BP target 130/80 mmHg or less, so increase the ACE inhibitor (perindopril) and check potassium and creatinine 1 to 2 weeks later. An SGLT2 inhibitor is favoured for kidney and cardiovascular protection. Repeat the uACR, then check eGFR and uACR at least yearly.

rows.n: Concentration shown for calculation; interpret the ACR
Repeat to confirm: 2 of 3 samples over 3 months

ask: You are now handing over to your supervising GP. Please give an ISBAR handover of Jack Dickson, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Jack now, here in general practice.
Jack is now back in the room. Explain the results to him, answer his questions, and give him specific safety-netting advice.
expect:
• Identify: self, GP registrar; Jack Dickson, 57.
  • Situation: annual diabetes review. Poor control with new microvascular complications.
  • Background: type 2 diabetes for 11 years, on metformin XR and glargine 30 units (same thigh site, lipohypertrophy). Hypertension and high cholesterol. Smokes 10 a day, 20 drinks a week. Last eye check 3 years ago (overdue).
  • Assessment: Retinal photos: microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages and cotton wool spots both eyes, no new vessels or foveal exudates, i.e. moderate NPDR. HbA1c 9.4% (79), up from 8.6%, well above 7.0%. LDL 3.3 normal-range but above the diabetes target of <2.0, with low HDL and high TG. ALT/GGT up, likely alcohol/MASLD; B12 and MCV normal. uACR 6.8 = moderately increased albuminuria, eGFR 76, needs 2 of 3 samples to confirm. Exam: stocking neuropathy with loss of protective sensation, pulses normal, callus, left interdigital tinea, left-thigh lipohypertrophy, BP 148/90.
  • Recommendation: Intensify glucose-lowering, ophthalmology and podiatry referral, repeat uACR; plan to follow.

Most likely: poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.4%) with microvascular complications:

  • moderate NPDR on the photographs;
  • peripheral neuropathy: stocking loss, monofilament not felt, absent ankle jerks;
  • probable diabetic kidney disease: uACR 6.8.

He also has high cardiovascular risk.

  • Hypertensive retinopathy: BP is raised, but there is no AV nipping or flame haemorrhages, and the microaneurysms and dot-blot pattern are diabetic.
  • Alcohol or B12-deficiency neuropathy: he drinks 20 a week with a raised GGT, but B12 and MCV are normal.
  • Sight-threatening retinopathy (proliferative or macular oedema): no new vessels or exudates, but OCT is needed.
  • PAD: he smokes, but pulses are palpable and he has no claudication.

1. Glucose: add an SGLT2 inhibitor (or a GLP-1 RA). Rotate sites away from the lipohypertrophy and use a new needle each time. Check glucose more often when changing sites and consider reducing glargine (e.g. 10 to 20%), especially when starting the SGLT2 inhibitor at the same time, then titrate to fasting readings. Diabetes educator.
  2. Eyes: non-urgent ophthalmology referral (seen within about 3 months) for dilated examination and OCT; review every 3 to 6 months as the ophthalmologist sets. Lower HbA1c steadily.
  3. Kidneys and BP: target 130/80 or less. Increase perindopril and check K and creatinine in 1 to 2 weeks. Repeat uACR.
  4. Feet: at risk from loss of protective sensation. Podiatry for callus and footwear; topical terbinafine for tinea. Credit: intermediate risk (RACGP) or IWGDF risk 1, low risk (Diabetes Feet Australia).
  5. Risk factors (credit): statin adherence then increase; Quitline or varenicline; alcohol 10 or fewer a week, no more than 4 a day.

• Complications in plain words: Eyes, kidneys, nerves; heart attack, stroke, leg circulation. Early eye and nerve changes already, kidney test needs repeating, no heart or stroke problems yet; eye disease caught early is treatable.
  • Feet: check daily, no barefoot; any cut, blister, redness, swelling or colour change: review within a day (same day if hot, red or swollen); fever or a cold, pale, painful foot: ED.
  • Eyes: sudden loss of vision, a shower of floaters or a curtain: same-day eye review or ED.
  • Hypos: carry jellybeans or soft drink, not a muesli bar; drive only if above 5.

ddx.dx: Poorly controlled type 2 diabetes with microvascular complications (moderate non-proliferative retinopathy, peripheral neuropathy, early diabetic kidney disease)
ddx.for: Eleven years of diabetes with HbA1c 9.4%, microaneurysms, dot and blot haemorrhages and cotton wool spots, stocking sensory loss with absent ankle jerks, and uACR 6.8 mg/mmol.
His BP is 148/90 mmHg and he has cotton wool spots.
ddx.against: There is no arteriovenous nipping, arteriolar narrowing or flame haemorrhage, and the microaneurysms and dot and blot haemorrhages are the diabetic pattern.

ddx.dx: Alcohol-related or vitamin B12-deficiency peripheral neuropathy
ddx.for: He drinks about 20 standard drinks a week with a raised GGT, and has taken metformin for years.
ddx.against: His B12 and MCV are normal, and long-standing poor glycaemic control fully explains a symmetrical stocking neuropathy.

ddx.dx: Sight-threatening diabetic retinopathy (proliferative retinopathy or diabetic macular oedema)
ddx.for: HbA1c 9.4%, cotton wool spots, 3 years without an eye check, and acuity 6/9.
ddx.against: No new vessels, venous beading or exudates near the fovea, and acuity corrects to 6/6 with pinhole, but macular oedema needs OCT to exclude.

ddx.dx: Peripheral arterial disease with an at-risk foot
ddx.for: He smokes about 18 pack-years and has diabetes, hypertension and dyslipidaemia; diabetes can hide claudication when sensation is lost.
ddx.against: His pedal and popliteal pulses are palpable, capillary refill is under 2 seconds, hair is normal and he has no claudication. Palpable pulses do not fully exclude PAD in diabetes, so consider ABI/TBI if pulses are reduced, symptoms develop or a wound occurs.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. The examination is targeted at the lower limbs. If the candidate asks about visual acuity or fundoscopy, give the acuity and say the retinal photograph will be given in Part 2; this is not marked in Part 1. Jack reveals his injection habits only when asked how and where he injects, and his fear about his father's toe only when his feet are discussed.

In Part 2 hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Questions 1 to 3 are a handover and discussion with the supervising GP, so Jack stays silent. For Question 4 Jack is back in the room and the person playing him puts his Part 2 questions while the candidate explains. His question "What else can this diabetes do to me?" earns the complications item under Safety netting.

Foot risk: accept either intermediate risk (RACGP handbook, review every 3 to 6 months) or IWGDF risk 1, low risk (Diabetes Feet Australia, review every 6 to 12 months). Credit, but do not require: 000 for chest pain or stroke symptoms; addressing his erectile dysfunction; excluding transient causes of a raised uACR.

A high-performing candidate covers control, hypos, insulin technique and every complication system in the history. They examine the feet properly, including between the toes and the heels, with a monofilament, tuning fork, reflexes and pulses, and they find the lipohypertrophy. In Part 2 they grade the retinopathy, see that a "normal" LDL is above target, recognise albuminuria needing confirmation, warn about hypos when he moves his injection site, and give a structured plan with specific red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a generic history and does not ask how he injects. They skip the monofilament or leave the socks on, or call the retinopathy "hypertensive". They miss the albuminuria, or give vague safety netting such as "come back if worse".
explain:
The annual cycle of care

Every person with diabetes should have a structured review at least once a year (RACGP handbook). It covers:

  • HbA1c (at least every 6 to 12 months, more often when it is above target);
  • BP, weight, BMI and waist;
  • lipids;
  • eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio;
  • an eye examination at least every 2 years, yearly in higher-risk people, and more often once retinopathy is present (mild NPDR yearly, moderate NPDR every 3 to 6 months);
  • a foot risk assessment;
  • smoking, alcohol, diet and physical activity;
  • a medication review, including adherence and injection technique.

Jack's review finds complications in three organs, and his last eye check was 3 years ago (overdue).

Long-term complications of poorly controlled diabetes

  • Microvascular: retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy (peripheral and autonomic, including erectile dysfunction).
  • Macrovascular: coronary disease, cerebrovascular disease and peripheral vascular disease.

Jack has all three microvascular complications. His smoking, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, albuminuria and family history put him at high cardiovascular risk.

Diabetic retinopathy

Microaneurysms, dot and blot haemorrhages and cotton wool spots, without new vessels, are non-proliferative retinopathy.

  • Mild: microaneurysms only.
  • Moderate: more than microaneurysms alone but short of severe.
  • Severe (4-2-1 rule): severe haemorrhages and microaneurysms in all four quadrants, venous beading in two or more quadrants, or IRMA in at least one quadrant.
  • Proliferative: new vessels, which can bleed or cause retinal detachment.

Jack's is moderate. Maculopathy (macular oedema) can occur at any stage and causes most vision loss. Photographs cannot exclude it, so he needs an ophthalmologist for a dilated examination and OCT, then review every 3 to 6 months. Hypertensive retinopathy gives arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nipping, flame haemorrhages and, when severe, disc swelling. Better glucose and BP control slows progression. A rapid large fall in HbA1c can transiently worsen retinopathy, so lower it steadily and tell the ophthalmologist about treatment changes.

Neuropathy and the at-risk foot

A symmetrical stocking loss with an absent monofilament, reduced vibration and absent ankle jerks is distal symmetrical polyneuropathy. Alcohol and B12 deficiency (metformin) are the main mimics. His normal B12 and MCV make B12 deficiency unlikely, but drinking less helps both his nerves and his liver.

Loss of protective sensation with palpable pulses, no deformity and no previous ulcer is intermediate risk in the RACGP handbook (review every 3 to 6 months) and IWGDF risk 1, low risk, in Diabetes Feet Australia (review every 6 to 12 months).

Callus on an insensate foot shows high pressure and is a pre-ulcerative sign. Interdigital tinea breaks the skin and lets bacteria in. Both need treatment. Lipohypertrophy from injecting the same site absorbs insulin erratically, which worsens control and causes unpredictable hypos. Rotate sites and use a new needle each time (see the hypoglycaemia warning below).

Kidneys and cardiovascular risk

A uACR above 2.5 mg/mmol in men (3.5 in women) is raised. Moderately increased albuminuria needs 2 of 3 samples over 3 months to confirm. With eGFR 76 this would be CKD G2 A2 (Kidney Health Australia). Management:

  • an ACE inhibitor or ARB titrated to the maximum tolerated dose, with BP 130/80 mmHg or less;
  • an SGLT2 inhibitor for kidney and cardiovascular protection;
  • yearly eGFR and uACR.

An LDL of 3.3 mmol/L sits inside the lab's general range but above the RACGP diabetes target (below 2.0), so the statin should be increased. Low HDL with high triglycerides is the typical atherogenic pattern of insulin resistance.

Glycaemic management

The general HbA1c target is 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) or less, individualised to the person.

  • SGLT2 inhibitor: favoured with albuminuria or cardiovascular risk. Teach sick-day rules: stop it when unwell, fasting or before surgery, because of the risk of ketoacidosis, which can occur with a near-normal glucose. Keep taking insulin and check glucose more often. If vomiting or dehydrated, also withhold metformin and perindopril until eating and drinking normally; stop the SGLT2 inhibitor 3 days before surgery or a procedure (ADS).
  • GLP-1 receptor agonist: an alternative that also helps with weight.
  • Insulin: moving injections from the lipohypertrophy into healthy tissue increases insulin absorption and can cause hypoglycaemia, and Jack already has hypos. Check glucose more often when changing sites and consider reducing glargine (e.g. by 10 to 20%), especially when starting the SGLT2 inhibitor at the same time, then titrate to fasting readings once the technique is fixed.

Support him with a diabetes educator, a dietitian and an exercise physiologist under a GP chronic condition management plan. Help him quit smoking (Quitline, varenicline) and cut alcohol to no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day (NHMRC).

Diagnosing type 2 diabetes (background)

Any one of the following diagnoses diabetes:

  • HbA1c 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more;
  • fasting glucose 7.0 mmol/L or more;
  • random glucose 11.1 mmol/L or more with symptoms;
  • 2-hour glucose on an oral glucose tolerance test of 11.1 mmol/L or more.

Without symptoms, a second abnormal test on another day is needed.

Safety netting

  • Feet: new wounds need GP review within a day. A hot, red or swollen foot (infection or active Charcot foot) needs same-day review. Fever with spreading redness, or a cold, pale, painful foot (ischaemia), needs ED.
  • Eyes: sudden visual loss, floaters or a curtain (vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment) needs same-day eye assessment.
  • Driving: because he is on insulin, he should check his glucose before driving and drive only if it is above 5. As an insulin-treated driver he also has licensing obligations under Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive, and should carry fast-acting carbohydrate in the car.

Hypos, driving and follow-up

  • Treat a hypo with 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (for example 6 or 7 jellybeans or 150 mL of regular soft drink), recheck in 15 minutes, then have a carbohydrate snack.
  • As an insulin-treated driver he has licensing obligations under the Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive standards, and should carry fast-acting carbohydrate in the car.
  • Chest pain or stroke symptoms mean calling 000.
  • Review in 1 to 2 weeks for BP, potassium and creatinine; repeat uACR and HbA1c at 3 months.
points: The annual cycle of care covers HbA1c, BP, weight, lipids, eGFR and uACR, an eye check (more often once retinopathy is present: every 3 to 6 months for moderate NPDR), a foot risk assessment, lifestyle and a medication review that includes how insulin is injected.

Microaneurysms, dot and blot haemorrhages and cotton wool spots without new vessels are non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Refer to an ophthalmologist, because photographs cannot exclude macular oedema.

A 10 g monofilament not felt (with or without loss of vibration) means loss of protective sensation; absent ankle jerks support the neuropathy. With palpable pulses and no deformity or ulcer history this is intermediate risk (RACGP) or IWGDF risk 1, low risk (Diabetes Feet Australia): arrange podiatry, treat callus and tinea, and teach daily foot checks.
Confirm a raised uACR (above 2.5 mg/mmol in men) on 2 of 3 samples. With albuminuria, aim for BP 130/80 mmHg or less on a titrated ACE inhibitor or ARB, and favour an SGLT2 inhibitor.
An LDL inside the laboratory range can still be above the target for a person with diabetes (below 2.0 mmol/L).
Lipohypertrophy from injecting the same site causes erratic insulin absorption and poor control. Rotate sites and use a new needle each time.
